claims.claim: People with more positive self-perceptions of ageing lived 7.5 years longer in one cohort of 660.
claims.supporting_passage: This research found that older individuals with more positive self-perceptions of aging, measured up to 23 years earlier, lived 7.5 years longer than those with less positive self-perceptions of aging. This advantage remained after age, gender, socioeconomic status, loneliness, and functional health were included as covariates. ... The sample consisted of 660 individuals aged 50 and older who participated in a community-based survey, the Ohio Longitudinal Study of Aging and Retirement (OLSAR).
claims.pico_timeframe: 660 Ohio residents aged 50+; exposure: self-perceptions of ageing measured once; comparator: less positive; outcome: survival; up to 23 years
claims.safe_wording: In one US study of 660 people aged 50 and over, those with more positive views of their own ageing lived on average 7.5 years longer, after adjusting for age, sex, income, loneliness and health. This is a link, not proof of cause.
claims.qualifications: Observational; single cohort; adjusted; do not say 'because of'; title's word 'increased' is the authors' causal framing.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Reverse causation (unmeasured illness) and residual confounding possible; later pooled evidence shows a small effect.

numbers.meaning: adjusted survival difference, more vs less positive self-perceptions

claims.claim: Meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal studies found a small significant effect, stronger with shorter follow-up and younger samples.
claims.supporting_passage: A systematic search ... resulted in 19 longitudinal studies ... The analyses revealed heterogeneity, with stronger effects for studies with a shorter period of follow-up, for studies of health versus survival, for studies with younger participants ... Subjective aging has a small significant effect on health, health behaviors, and survival.
claims.pico_timeframe: 19 longitudinal studies, mean ages 57-85; subjective ageing; health, behaviours, survival
claims.safe_wording: When 19 long-term studies were pooled, how people view their own ageing had a small link with later health and survival, weaker with longer follow-up.
claims.qualifications: Keep 'small'; effect larger for health than survival.

numbers.meaning: pooled likelihood ratio; do not translate for public

claims.claim: Association may reflect reverse causation and confounding; the case against ageism is ethical.
claims.supporting_passage: (methods interpretation; no source needed as general point; ethical position marked as judgement)
claims.safe_wording: Studies like this cannot rule out that people who were already less well viewed ageing more negatively. We should oppose ageist treatment because it is unfair, whatever the survival figure.
claims.qualifications: State as interpretation and judgement, not finding.

claims.claim: Glass 1998 described discordance between hypothetical and enacted function in MacArthur data.
claims.supporting_passage: Failure to attend to this distinction has obscured considerable discordance between what people say they are able to do in standard functional disability assessments, and what they actually do at home. To illustrate this point, data from the MacArthur Studies of Successful Aging comparing the hypothetical to the enacted tenses are presented. These data show a consistent pattern of discordance between these two tenses.
claims.pico_timeframe: Older adults, MacArthur Studies; hypothetical vs enacted (and experimental) function
claims.safe_wording: A 1998 paper described three 'tenses' of function: what people say they can do, what they do in a test, and what they actually do at home. In US data, what people said they could do and what they did at home showed 'a consistent pattern of discordance'.
claims.qualifications: No numbers available; do not quantify.

claims.claim: Self-reported and performance-based function agree only moderately in older people.
claims.supporting_passage: Cross-modal agreement was moderate, with by-criterion and frailty-wide Kappa statistics of 0.55-0.60 in all cases. ... Commonly used self-reported disability items cannot be assumed to stand in for performance-based criteria in the PFP. [Owens 2002:] Disagreement between the self-reported and performance-based measure of function was common (slight disagreement, 55.0%; substantial disagreement, 19.3%). Most women (95.4%) overreported their level of function.
claims.pico_timeframe: CHS older adults (n=5888) self-report vs grip/walk tests; post-stroke women (n=620) Barthel vs Physical Performance Test
claims.safe_wording: In a large US study of older adults, self-reported walking and strength difficulty agreed only moderately with measured tests, and one could not simply stand in for the other.
claims.qualifications: Owens is post-stroke women only; do not generalise its percentages.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Direction of disagreement varies by study.

numbers.meaning: moderate agreement, CHS; practitioner post only
of women who disagreed/overall overreported, post-stroke cohort only

claims.claim: WHO ICF distinguishes capacity from performance.
claims.supporting_passage: Not opened (WHO document not accessible from this environment).
claims.safe_wording: Omit or state without attributing to WHO.

claims.claim: Newcastle 85+: median diseases women 5, men 4; 77.6% rated health compared with others their age good or better.
claims.supporting_passage: Overall, 77.6% (646/832) of participants rated their health compared with others of the same age as good, very good, or excellent. ... Women had significantly higher disease counts (medians: women 5, men 4; P=0.033) ... This large cohort of 85 year olds showed good levels of both self rated health and functional ability despite significant levels of disease and impairment.
claims.pico_timeframe: People aged 85 (born 1921), Newcastle/North Tyneside, including care homes; baseline 2006-07 cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a study of 85-year-olds in Newcastle, the typical woman had 5 recorded diseases and the typical man 4, yet about 3 in 4 (78 in 100) rated their health as good, very good or excellent compared with others their age.
claims.qualifications: Keep 'compared with others their age'; do not say disease lists 'say little' about life; cross-sectional.

numbers.meaning: rated health good or better vs peers

claims.claim: Most common conditions hypertension and osteoarthritis; hearing impairment ~60%.
claims.supporting_passage: The most prevalent diseases were hypertension (57.5%, 592/1030) and osteoarthritis (51.8%, 534/1030). ... hearing impairment in 59.6% (505/848)
claims.safe_wording: The commonest recorded conditions were high blood pressure (in over half) and osteoarthritis (about half); about 6 in 10 had hearing impairment.

claims.claim: Time to benefit of screening can exceed remaining life, a legitimate reason for different advice.
claims.supporting_passage: On average across included studies, it took 10.7 years (4.4 to 21.6) before one death from breast cancer was prevented for 1000 women screened. ... it took 10.3 years (6.0 to 16.4) before one death from colorectal cancer was prevented for 1000 patients screened. Our results suggest that screening for breast and colorectal cancer is most appropriate for patients with a life expectancy greater than 10 years.
claims.pico_timeframe: Screened adults >40 in RCTs; screening vs none; cancer death; time to benefit
claims.safe_wording: For breast and bowel cancer screening, it took about 10 years before 1 death was prevented for every 1000 people screened, so researchers suggest screening suits people expected to live more than 10 years. That is a reason about expected benefit, not about age itself.
claims.qualifications: Screening-specific example; life expectancy, not age, is the criterion.

numbers.meaning: time until 1 cancer death prevented per 1000 screened

claims.claim: Age-based differences in access to treatment are widely documented.
claims.supporting_passage: Ageism led to significantly worse health outcomes in 95.5% of the studies and 74.0% of the 1,159 ageism-health associations examined.
claims.pico_timeframe: 422 studies; ageism (structural and individual) vs health outcomes
claims.safe_wording: Omit, or say only that a large review found ageism linked with worse health in many studies worldwide, without causal wording.
claims.qualifications: Review does not isolate treatment access in the abstract; causal wording must not be borrowed.

claims.claim: Age discrimination in services unlawful in GB since Oct 2012 unless objectively justified.
claims.supporting_passage: Not opened; official legislation pages not accessible.

claims.claim: In >100,000 IAPT patients, older adults were more likely to recover (crude and adjusted) and less likely to drop out.
claims.supporting_passage: At the end of treatment, older adults were more likely to reliably recover (52.5% vs 40.9%,<0.001), reliably improve (72% vs 66.4%,<0.001), and attrition was less likely (18.1% vs 31.6%,<0.001) compared to working-age adults. ... In adjusted models older adults were more likely to reliably recover (OR=1.33(95%CI=1.24-1.43)) ... There are potential selection biases affecting the characteristics of older people attending these services. Residual confounding cannot be ruled out
claims.pico_timeframe: 100,179 patients with depression/anxiety, 8 London IAPT services, 2008-2019; 65+ vs 18-64; reliable recovery, attrition at end of treatment
claims.safe_wording: In NHS talking therapy services in London, about 53 in 100 people aged 65+ recovered, compared with 41 in 100 working-age adults, and fewer dropped out (18 vs 32 in 100). The difference held after allowing for how unwell people were at the start, but older people who reach these services may be a selected group.
claims.qualifications: Observational; London services; after matching, the recovery advantage for depression alone was not clear (anxiety drove the effect).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Earlier meta-analyses found similar efficacy across ages for depression.

claims.claim: Older adults are under-represented in these services.
claims.supporting_passage: We found that older people accounted for just 3.8% of patients treated at the services. This suggests that older adults were under-represented in the services that provided data here as over 65 year olds account for approximately 18% of the population ().
claims.safe_wording: In these London services, fewer than 4 in 100 people treated were 65 or over, although about 18 in 100 of the population are that age.
claims.qualifications: The 18% population figure is cited background; comparison is crude (need, not just population share, matters). National NHS Digital report not opened.

claims.claim: Self-referral in England; different routes in Scotland.
claims.supporting_passage: Not opened; official pages not accessible.
claims.safe_wording: Omit specific referral routes; may say 'ask your GP about talking therapy'.

candidates.reason: Levy 2002 and Westerhof 2014 abstracts support the claims with 'linked with' wording; closing is marked judgement.
Glass 1998 wording supported (use 'discordance'); moderate self-report vs performance agreement from Bandeen-Roche 2023. ICF claim not verified and must be omitted or unattributed.
All figures in Collerton 2009 abstract; must keep 'compared with others their age' and drop 'says little'.
Equality Act claim could not be opened; access-to-treatment claim not supported as worded by Chang 2020 abstract.
candidates.revised_angle: Build the post on the question itself plus one legitimate age-linked reason (time to benefit of screening, Lee 2013: about 10 years), framed as judgement that you are entitled to hear the reasons; no legal claim, no ageism-prevalence statistic.

candidates.reason: Crude and adjusted outcomes and under-representation in Saunders 2021 full text; referral-route claim unverified, so omit specific routes.
